messages.content:
Below is a **complete, linear mixed‑integer programming (MILP) formulation** for Conflict‑Detection‑and‑Resolution (CDR) in a railway network that uses **Distance‑to‑Go (DTG) signalling (ETCS Level 2)**.  
The model extends the usual fixed‑block formulation by (i) using **speed‑dependent braking distances** and (ii) introducing **train‑specific Brake‑Indication‑Points (BIP)** that must be respected when a train follows another one.

---

## 1.  Sets and Indices  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| $\mathcal I$ | Set of trains, indexed by $i$ |
| $\mathcal S$ | Set of track sections (blocks), indexed by $s$ |
| $\mathcal R_i$ | Set of admissible routes for train $i$, indexed by $k$ |
| $\mathcal P_{i,k}\subseteq\mathcal S$ | Ordered list of sections that compose route $k$ for train $i$ |
| $\mathcal V_{i,s}$ | Discrete speed options that train $i$ may use in section $s$, indexed by $v$ |
| $\mathcal J_i$ | Set of trains that can ever share a section with train $i$ (i.e. $j\in\mathcal J_i$ if $\exists s$ with $s\in\mathcal P_{i,k}$ and $s\in\mathcal P_{j,\ell}$ for some $k,\ell$) |

---

## 2.  Parameters  

| Symbol | Meaning | Typical unit |
|--------|---------|--------------|
| $T^{\text{sch}}_{i,s}$ | Scheduled time at the **end** of section $s$ for train $i$ | s |
| $D_{i,s}$ | Physical length of section $s$ (for train $i$) | m |
| $L_{i,s}$ | Length of the **Brake‑Indication‑Point** (BIP) of train $i$ measured from the downstream end of section $s$ (the distance that must be cleared before the following train can enter) | m |
| $B_i(v)$ | Braking distance of train $i$ when travelling at speed $v$ (parameter, pre‑computed from the train’s braking curve) | m |
| $V_{i,s}^{v}$ | Speed value (in m/s) of option $v\in\mathcal V_{i,s}$ | m/s |
| $M$ | Large positive constant (big‑M) – must dominate any feasible time difference (e.g. $M=10^5$ s) |
| $\Delta^{\text{min}}$ | Minimum admissible headway (e.g. signalling reaction time) | s |
| $c_{i}$ | Penalty weight for train $i$’s delay (usually $c_i=1$) | – |

---

## 3.  Decision Variables  

| Symbol | Type | Meaning |
|--------|------|---------|
| $a_{i,s}\ge 0$ | Continuous | **Actual arrival time** of train $i$ at the **down‑stream end** of section $s$ |
| $d_{i,s}\ge 0$ | Continuous | **Actual departure time** of train $i$ from the **up‑stream end** of section $s$ (i.e. the time it clears the section) |
| $v_{i,s}^{v}\in\{0,1\}$ | Binary | 1 if train $i$ uses speed option $v$ in section $s$, 0 otherwise (only one speed per section) |
| $r_{i,k}\in\{0,1\}$ | Binary | 1 if train $i$ follows route $k\in\mathcal R_i$, 0 otherwise |
| $z_{i,j,s}\in\{0,1\}$ | Binary | 1 if **train $i$ precedes train $j$** on section $s$ (i.e. $i$ is ahead of $j$), 0 otherwise |
| $u_{i,j,s}\in\{0,1\}$ | Binary | 1 if **both** trains $i$ and $j$ occupy section $s$ (used to activate the separation constraint only when they share the section) |

---

## 4.  Objective  

Minimise total (weighted) delay at the final destination of every train  

\[
\boxed{
\min \; \sum_{i\in\mathcal I} c_i\Bigl(a_{i,s_i^{\text{dest}}}-T^{\text{sch}}_{i,s_i^{\text{dest}}}\Bigr)
}
\]

where $s_i^{\text{dest}}$ is the last section of the route actually selected for train $i$ (the destination section).

---

## 5.  Model Constraints  

### 5.1  Route‑selection  

\[
\sum_{k\in\mathcal R_i} r_{i,k}=1 \qquad\forall i\in\mathcal I \tag{R1}
\]

### 5.2  Section‑membership linking  

A train can only have timing variables on sections that belong to the chosen route.

\[
a_{i,s}\le M\Bigl(\sum_{k\in\mathcal R_i} r_{i,k}\,\mathbf 1_{s\in\mathcal P_{i,k}}\Bigr) \qquad\forall i,s \tag{R2}
\]
\[
d_{i,s}\le M\Bigl(\sum_{k\in\mathcal R_i} r_{i,k}\,\mathbf 1_{s\in\mathcal P_{i,k}}\Bigr) \qquad\forall i,s \tag{R3}
\]

(If $s$ does **not** belong to the selected route, the RHS becomes 0 and the variables are forced to 0.)

### 5.3  Exactly one speed option per traversed section  

\[
\sum_{v\in\mathcal V_{i,s}} v_{i,s}^{v}= \sum_{k\in\mathcal R_i} r_{i,k}\,\mathbf 1_{s\in\mathcal P_{i,k}} \qquad\forall i,s \tag{S1}
\]

Thus a speed is chosen **iff** the section is travelled.

### 5.4  Time‑distance consistency (travel time)  

For each train and each traversed section $s$ (with predecessor section $p(s)$ in the chosen route)

\[
a_{i,s}\;\ge\; d_{i,p(s)}\;+\;\sum_{v\in\mathcal V_{i,s}} \frac{D_{i,s}}{V_{i,s}^{v}}\,v_{i,s}^{v} \qquad\forall i,\;s\in\mathcal P_{i,k},\;k\in\mathcal R_i \tag{T1}
\]

If a section is the first one of a route, $d_{i,p(s)}$ is replaced by the train’s scheduled departure from its origin (or a given release time).

### 5.5  Minimum dwell / clearance inside a section  

A train must stay in a section at least long enough to travel it at the chosen speed, plus a small signalling reaction time $\Delta^{\text{min}}$:

\[
d_{i,s}\;\ge\; a_{i,s}\;+\;\Delta^{\text{min}} \qquad\forall i,s \tag{T2}
\]

### 5.6  Co‑existence indicator  

\[
u_{i,j,s}\;\ge\; z_{i,j,s} \qquad\forall i<j,\;s\in\mathcal S \tag{U1}
\]
\[
u_{i,j,s}\;\ge\; z_{j,i,s} \qquad\forall i<j,\;s\in\mathcal S \tag{U2}
\]
\[
u_{i,j,s}\;\le\; z_{i,j,s}+z_{j,i,s} \qquad\forall i<j,\;s\in\mathcal S \tag{U3}
\]

Thus $u_{i,j,s}=1$ exactly when the two trains use the same section (the ordering variables become relevant only then).

### 5.7  Ordering (precedence) on a shared section  

For every unordered pair of trains that may share a section:

\[
z_{i,j,s}+z_{j,i,s}=u_{i,j,s}\qquad\forall i<j,\;s\in\mathcal S \tag{O1}
\]

If the section is not shared ($u_{i,j,s}=0$) both ordering binaries are forced to 0.

### 5.8  **DTG safety separation – core enhancement**  

When train $i$ follows train $j$ on section $s$ ($z_{j,i,s}=1$) the **arrival** of $i$ must be delayed enough so that, even if $i$ brakes at the speed it will use in $s$, it can stop **before** the **Brake‑Indication‑Point** of $j$ (i.e. before $j$’s *end‑of‑authority*).  
The required time head‑way is the **braking time** needed to cover the distance $B_i(V_{i,s})+L_{j,s}$, where $L_{j,s}$ is the BIP length of the leading train.

Because $B_i(v)$ and $L_{j,s}$ are parameters, the head‑way can be expressed linearly as a *time* using the speed actually chosen by train $i$:

\[
\underbrace{\frac{B_i\!\bigl(V_{i,s}^{v}\bigr)+L_{j,s}}{V_{i,s}^{v}}}_{\displaystyle \text{Braking\;time for option }v}
\;\;=\;\; \tau_{i,s}^{v}\quad\forall v\in\mathcal V_{i,s}
\]

(Pre‑compute $\tau_{i,s}^{v}$ for every train, section and speed option.)

The DTG separation constraint becomes

\[
a_{i,s}\;\ge\; a_{j,s}\;+\;\sum_{v\in\mathcal V_{i,s}}\tau_{i,s}^{v}\,v_{i,s}^{v}
\;-\;M\bigl(1-z_{j,i,s}\bigr) \qquad\forall i\neq j,\;s\in\mathcal S \tag{D1}
\]

Explanation:

* If $z_{j,i,s}=1$ (i follows $j$) the big‑M term disappears and the inequality enforces the required braking‑time head‑way.  
* If $z_{j,i,s}=0$ the RHS is reduced by $M$, making the constraint non‑binding.

A symmetric version for the opposite order is automatically covered by the pair of constraints generated for the ordered pair $(i,j)$ and $(j,i)$.

### 5.9  No‑overlap in the same physical space (optional tighter bound)  

Because the DTG rule already guarantees that the following train can stop before the BIP of the leading train, an additional “one‑train‑per‑section” constraint is not strictly needed.  
If the practitioner still wants an explicit occupancy limit (e.g. to model signalling system capacity), the classic big‑M formulation can be added:

\[
d_{i,s}\;\le\; a_{j,s}\;-\;\Delta^{\text{min}} \;+\;M\bigl(1-z_{i,j,s}\bigr) \qquad\forall i\neq j,\;s\in\mathcal S \tag{O2}
\]

Together with (O1) this forces the two trains to be temporally separated by at least $\Delta^{\text{min}}$ when they are ordered.

### 5.10  Destination‑time definition (for the objective)  

Let $s_i^{\text{dest}}$ be the last section of the selected route of train $i$:

\[
s_i^{\text{dest}} = \sum_{k\in\mathcal R_i} k_{\text{last}}\,r_{i,k} \qquad\forall i\in\mathcal I
\]

where $k_{\text{last}}$ is the index of the last section in route $k$.  
Then the objective uses $a_{i,s_i^{\text{dest}}}$ as defined above.

---

## 6.  Summary of the Linear MILP  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;&\sum_{i\in\mathcal I} c_i\bigl(a_{i,s_i^{\text{dest}}}-T^{\text{sch}}_{i,s_i^{\text{dest}}}\bigr)\\[4pt]
\text{s.t. } &\text{(R1)–(R3)} &&\text{route selection and section activation}\\
&\text{(S1)} &&\text{exactly one speed per traversed section}\\
&\text{(T1)} &&\text{travel‑time consistency}\\
&\text{(T2)} &&\text{minimum dwell / clearance}\\
&\text{(U1)–(U3), (O1)} &&\text{co‑existence and ordering binaries}\\
&\text{(D1)} &&\text{DTG safety separation (core enhancement)}\\
&\text{(O2)} &&\text{optional explicit occupancy limit}\\
& a_{i,s},d_{i,s}\ge 0,\; v_{i,s}^{v},r_{i,k},z_{i,j,s},u_{i,j,s}\in\{0,1\}.
\end{aligned}
\]

All constraints are **linear**; the only non‑linear looking elements are the products $ \tau_{i,s}^{v}\,v_{i,s}^{v}$, but $v_{i,s}^{v}$ is binary, so the product is linear (a weighted sum of constants). The big‑M terms keep the model mixed‑integer.

---

## 7.  How the Model Captures the DTG Features  

| Feature | How it appears in the formulation |
|--------|-----------------------------------|
| **Speed‑dependent braking distance** | Parameter $B_i(v)$ (or pre‑computed $\tau_{i,s}^{v}$) is used inside constraint (D1). The head‑way depends on the *actual* speed chosen for the following train. |
| **Brake‑Indication‑Point (BIP)** | Parameter $L_{j,s}$ (distance from the downstream end of section $s$ that the leading train must clear) is added to the braking distance of the following train, again inside (D1). |
| **Dynamic separation (DTG)** | Instead of a fixed block count, (D1) enforces a **time head‑way** equal to the time needed for the following train to brake over $B_i(v)+L_{j,s}$, i.e. a true distance‑to‑go safety margin. |
| **Re‑ordering** | Binary $z_{i,j,s}$ decides which train is ahead on a shared section. The model can flip the order (by changing $z$) to resolve conflicts. |
| **Rerouting** | Binary $r_{i,k}$ chooses a route; the set of sections that become active for a train is linked to $r_{i,k}$ (constraints R2‑R3). |
| **Delay minimisation** | Objective penalises the difference between the actual arrival at the destination and the scheduled arrival, encouraging the solver to keep trains as close as possible to the timetable while respecting DTG safety. |

---

## 8.  Practical Modelling Tips  

1. **Big‑M sizing** – Choose $M$ just large enough to dominate the longest possible schedule deviation (e.g. $M = 10^4$ s). Too large values harm numerical stability.  
2. **Pre‑computation of $\tau$** – For every train $i$, section $s$, and speed option $v$, compute  
   \[
   \tau_{i,s}^{v}= \frac{B_i(V_{i,s}^{v})+L_{\text{max}}}{V_{i,s}^{v}}
   \]  
   where $L_{\text{max}}$ is the longest BIP among all trains that may be ahead on $s$. This keeps the model linear.  
3. **Sparse pair set** – In realistic networks only a tiny fraction of train pairs ever share a section; generate $\mathcal J_i$ accordingly to keep the number of $z$ and $u$ variables manageable.  
4. **Route‑specific BIPs** – If a BIP length depends on the route (e.g. different switch geometry), store $L_{j,s,k}$ and use the selected route binary $r_{j,k}$ to pick the correct value inside (D1).  
5. **Extensions** – The model can be enriched with (i) energy‑optimal speed selection, (ii) platform dwell‑time windows, (iii) passenger‑connection penalties – all by adding linear terms or additional binary variables without changing the DTG core.  

---

### End of formulation  

The MILP above provides a **linear, solvable** representation of conflict detection and resolution under ETCS Level‑2 DTG signalling, explicitly accounting for **speed‑dependent braking distances** and **train‑specific brake‑indication points**, while still allowing **re‑ordering** and **rerouting** decisions to minimise overall delay.

response.content:
Below is a **complete, linear mixed‑integer programming (MILP) formulation** for Conflict‑Detection‑and‑Resolution (CDR) in a railway network that uses **Distance‑to‑Go (DTG) signalling (ETCS Level 2)**.  
The model extends the usual fixed‑block formulation by (i) using **speed‑dependent braking distances** and (ii) introducing **train‑specific Brake‑Indication‑Points (BIP)** that must be respected when a train follows another one.

---

## 1.  Sets and Indices  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| $\mathcal I$ | Set of trains, indexed by $i$ |
| $\mathcal S$ | Set of track sections (blocks), indexed by $s$ |
| $\mathcal R_i$ | Set of admissible routes for train $i$, indexed by $k$ |
| $\mathcal P_{i,k}\subseteq\mathcal S$ | Ordered list of sections that compose route $k$ for train $i$ |
| $\mathcal V_{i,s}$ | Discrete speed options that train $i$ may use in section $s$, indexed by $v$ |
| $\mathcal J_i$ | Set of trains that can ever share a section with train $i$ (i.e. $j\in\mathcal J_i$ if $\exists s$ with $s\in\mathcal P_{i,k}$ and $s\in\mathcal P_{j,\ell}$ for some $k,\ell$) |

---

## 2.  Parameters  

| Symbol | Meaning | Typical unit |
|--------|---------|--------------|
| $T^{\text{sch}}_{i,s}$ | Scheduled time at the **end** of section $s$ for train $i$ | s |
| $D_{i,s}$ | Physical length of section $s$ (for train $i$) | m |
| $L_{i,s}$ | Length of the **Brake‑Indication‑Point** (BIP) of train $i$ measured from the downstream end of section $s$ (the distance that must be cleared before the following train can enter) | m |
| $B_i(v)$ | Braking distance of train $i$ when travelling at speed $v$ (parameter, pre‑computed from the train’s braking curve) | m |
| $V_{i,s}^{v}$ | Speed value (in m/s) of option $v\in\mathcal V_{i,s}$ | m/s |
| $M$ | Large positive constant (big‑M) – must dominate any feasible time difference (e.g. $M=10^5$ s) |
| $\Delta^{\text{min}}$ | Minimum admissible headway (e.g. signalling reaction time) | s |
| $c_{i}$ | Penalty weight for train $i$’s delay (usually $c_i=1$) | – |

---

## 3.  Decision Variables  

| Symbol | Type | Meaning |
|--------|------|---------|
| $a_{i,s}\ge 0$ | Continuous | **Actual arrival time** of train $i$ at the **down‑stream end** of section $s$ |
| $d_{i,s}\ge 0$ | Continuous | **Actual departure time** of train $i$ from the **up‑stream end** of section $s$ (i.e. the time it clears the section) |
| $v_{i,s}^{v}\in\{0,1\}$ | Binary | 1 if train $i$ uses speed option $v$ in section $s$, 0 otherwise (only one speed per section) |
| $r_{i,k}\in\{0,1\}$ | Binary | 1 if train $i$ follows route $k\in\mathcal R_i$, 0 otherwise |
| $z_{i,j,s}\in\{0,1\}$ | Binary | 1 if **train $i$ precedes train $j$** on section $s$ (i.e. $i$ is ahead of $j$), 0 otherwise |
| $u_{i,j,s}\in\{0,1\}$ | Binary | 1 if **both** trains $i$ and $j$ occupy section $s$ (used to activate the separation constraint only when they share the section) |

---

## 4.  Objective  

Minimise total (weighted) delay at the final destination of every train  

\[
\boxed{
\min \; \sum_{i\in\mathcal I} c_i\Bigl(a_{i,s_i^{\text{dest}}}-T^{\text{sch}}_{i,s_i^{\text{dest}}}\Bigr)
}
\]

where $s_i^{\text{dest}}$ is the last section of the route actually selected for train $i$ (the destination section).

---

## 5.  Model Constraints  

### 5.1  Route‑selection  

\[
\sum_{k\in\mathcal R_i} r_{i,k}=1 \qquad\forall i\in\mathcal I \tag{R1}
\]

### 5.2  Section‑membership linking  

A train can only have timing variables on sections that belong to the chosen route.

\[
a_{i,s}\le M\Bigl(\sum_{k\in\mathcal R_i} r_{i,k}\,\mathbf 1_{s\in\mathcal P_{i,k}}\Bigr) \qquad\forall i,s \tag{R2}
\]
\[
d_{i,s}\le M\Bigl(\sum_{k\in\mathcal R_i} r_{i,k}\,\mathbf 1_{s\in\mathcal P_{i,k}}\Bigr) \qquad\forall i,s \tag{R3}
\]

(If $s$ does **not** belong to the selected route, the RHS becomes 0 and the variables are forced to 0.)

### 5.3  Exactly one speed option per traversed section  

\[
\sum_{v\in\mathcal V_{i,s}} v_{i,s}^{v}= \sum_{k\in\mathcal R_i} r_{i,k}\,\mathbf 1_{s\in\mathcal P_{i,k}} \qquad\forall i,s \tag{S1}
\]

Thus a speed is chosen **iff** the section is travelled.

### 5.4  Time‑distance consistency (travel time)  

For each train and each traversed section $s$ (with predecessor section $p(s)$ in the chosen route)

\[
a_{i,s}\;\ge\; d_{i,p(s)}\;+\;\sum_{v\in\mathcal V_{i,s}} \frac{D_{i,s}}{V_{i,s}^{v}}\,v_{i,s}^{v} \qquad\forall i,\;s\in\mathcal P_{i,k},\;k\in\mathcal R_i \tag{T1}
\]

If a section is the first one of a route, $d_{i,p(s)}$ is replaced by the train’s scheduled departure from its origin (or a given release time).

### 5.5  Minimum dwell / clearance inside a section  

A train must stay in a section at least long enough to travel it at the chosen speed, plus a small signalling reaction time $\Delta^{\text{min}}$:

\[
d_{i,s}\;\ge\; a_{i,s}\;+\;\Delta^{\text{min}} \qquad\forall i,s \tag{T2}
\]

### 5.6  Co‑existence indicator  

\[
u_{i,j,s}\;\ge\; z_{i,j,s} \qquad\forall i<j,\;s\in\mathcal S \tag{U1}
\]
\[
u_{i,j,s}\;\ge\; z_{j,i,s} \qquad\forall i<j,\;s\in\mathcal S \tag{U2}
\]
\[
u_{i,j,s}\;\le\; z_{i,j,s}+z_{j,i,s} \qquad\forall i<j,\;s\in\mathcal S \tag{U3}
\]

Thus $u_{i,j,s}=1$ exactly when the two trains use the same section (the ordering variables become relevant only then).

### 5.7  Ordering (precedence) on a shared section  

For every unordered pair of trains that may share a section:

\[
z_{i,j,s}+z_{j,i,s}=u_{i,j,s}\qquad\forall i<j,\;s\in\mathcal S \tag{O1}
\]

If the section is not shared ($u_{i,j,s}=0$) both ordering binaries are forced to 0.

### 5.8  **DTG safety separation – core enhancement**  

When train $i$ follows train $j$ on section $s$ ($z_{j,i,s}=1$) the **arrival** of $i$ must be delayed enough so that, even if $i$ brakes at the speed it will use in $s$, it can stop **before** the **Brake‑Indication‑Point** of $j$ (i.e. before $j$’s *end‑of‑authority*).  
The required time head‑way is the **braking time** needed to cover the distance $B_i(V_{i,s})+L_{j,s}$, where $L_{j,s}$ is the BIP length of the leading train.

Because $B_i(v)$ and $L_{j,s}$ are parameters, the head‑way can be expressed linearly as a *time* using the speed actually chosen by train $i$:

\[
\underbrace{\frac{B_i\!\bigl(V_{i,s}^{v}\bigr)+L_{j,s}}{V_{i,s}^{v}}}_{\displaystyle \text{Braking\;time for option }v}
\;\;=\;\; \tau_{i,s}^{v}\quad\forall v\in\mathcal V_{i,s}
\]

(Pre‑compute $\tau_{i,s}^{v}$ for every train, section and speed option.)

The DTG separation constraint becomes

\[
a_{i,s}\;\ge\; a_{j,s}\;+\;\sum_{v\in\mathcal V_{i,s}}\tau_{i,s}^{v}\,v_{i,s}^{v}
\;-\;M\bigl(1-z_{j,i,s}\bigr) \qquad\forall i\neq j,\;s\in\mathcal S \tag{D1}
\]

Explanation:

* If $z_{j,i,s}=1$ (i follows $j$) the big‑M term disappears and the inequality enforces the required braking‑time head‑way.  
* If $z_{j,i,s}=0$ the RHS is reduced by $M$, making the constraint non‑binding.

A symmetric version for the opposite order is automatically covered by the pair of constraints generated for the ordered pair $(i,j)$ and $(j,i)$.

### 5.9  No‑overlap in the same physical space (optional tighter bound)  

Because the DTG rule already guarantees that the following train can stop before the BIP of the leading train, an additional “one‑train‑per‑section” constraint is not strictly needed.  
If the practitioner still wants an explicit occupancy limit (e.g. to model signalling system capacity), the classic big‑M formulation can be added:

\[
d_{i,s}\;\le\; a_{j,s}\;-\;\Delta^{\text{min}} \;+\;M\bigl(1-z_{i,j,s}\bigr) \qquad\forall i\neq j,\;s\in\mathcal S \tag{O2}
\]

Together with (O1) this forces the two trains to be temporally separated by at least $\Delta^{\text{min}}$ when they are ordered.

### 5.10  Destination‑time definition (for the objective)  

Let $s_i^{\text{dest}}$ be the last section of the selected route of train $i$:

\[
s_i^{\text{dest}} = \sum_{k\in\mathcal R_i} k_{\text{last}}\,r_{i,k} \qquad\forall i\in\mathcal I
\]

where $k_{\text{last}}$ is the index of the last section in route $k$.  
Then the objective uses $a_{i,s_i^{\text{dest}}}$ as defined above.

---

## 6.  Summary of the Linear MILP  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;&\sum_{i\in\mathcal I} c_i\bigl(a_{i,s_i^{\text{dest}}}-T^{\text{sch}}_{i,s_i^{\text{dest}}}\bigr)\\[4pt]
\text{s.t. } &\text{(R1)–(R3)} &&\text{route selection and section activation}\\
&\text{(S1)} &&\text{exactly one speed per traversed section}\\
&\text{(T1)} &&\text{travel‑time consistency}\\
&\text{(T2)} &&\text{minimum dwell / clearance}\\
&\text{(U1)–(U3), (O1)} &&\text{co‑existence and ordering binaries}\\
&\text{(D1)} &&\text{DTG safety separation (core enhancement)}\\
&\text{(O2)} &&\text{optional explicit occupancy limit}\\
& a_{i,s},d_{i,s}\ge 0,\; v_{i,s}^{v},r_{i,k},z_{i,j,s},u_{i,j,s}\in\{0,1\}.
\end{aligned}
\]

All constraints are **linear**; the only non‑linear looking elements are the products $ \tau_{i,s}^{v}\,v_{i,s}^{v}$, but $v_{i,s}^{v}$ is binary, so the product is linear (a weighted sum of constants). The big‑M terms keep the model mixed‑integer.

---

## 7.  How the Model Captures the DTG Features  

| Feature | How it appears in the formulation |
|--------|-----------------------------------|
| **Speed‑dependent braking distance** | Parameter $B_i(v)$ (or pre‑computed $\tau_{i,s}^{v}$) is used inside constraint (D1). The head‑way depends on the *actual* speed chosen for the following train. |
| **Brake‑Indication‑Point (BIP)** | Parameter $L_{j,s}$ (distance from the downstream end of section $s$ that the leading train must clear) is added to the braking distance of the following train, again inside (D1). |
| **Dynamic separation (DTG)** | Instead of a fixed block count, (D1) enforces a **time head‑way** equal to the time needed for the following train to brake over $B_i(v)+L_{j,s}$, i.e. a true distance‑to‑go safety margin. |
| **Re‑ordering** | Binary $z_{i,j,s}$ decides which train is ahead on a shared section. The model can flip the order (by changing $z$) to resolve conflicts. |
| **Rerouting** | Binary $r_{i,k}$ chooses a route; the set of sections that become active for a train is linked to $r_{i,k}$ (constraints R2‑R3). |
| **Delay minimisation** | Objective penalises the difference between the actual arrival at the destination and the scheduled arrival, encouraging the solver to keep trains as close as possible to the timetable while respecting DTG safety. |

---

## 8.  Practical Modelling Tips  

1. **Big‑M sizing** – Choose $M$ just large enough to dominate the longest possible schedule deviation (e.g. $M = 10^4$ s). Too large values harm numerical stability.  
2. **Pre‑computation of $\tau$** – For every train $i$, section $s$, and speed option $v$, compute  
   \[
   \tau_{i,s}^{v}= \frac{B_i(V_{i,s}^{v})+L_{\text{max}}}{V_{i,s}^{v}}
   \]  
   where $L_{\text{max}}$ is the longest BIP among all trains that may be ahead on $s$. This keeps the model linear.  
3. **Sparse pair set** – In realistic networks only a tiny fraction of train pairs ever share a section; generate $\mathcal J_i$ accordingly to keep the number of $z$ and $u$ variables manageable.  
4. **Route‑specific BIPs** – If a BIP length depends on the route (e.g. different switch geometry), store $L_{j,s,k}$ and use the selected route binary $r_{j,k}$ to pick the correct value inside (D1).  
5. **Extensions** – The model can be enriched with (i) energy‑optimal speed selection, (ii) platform dwell‑time windows, (iii) passenger‑connection penalties – all by adding linear terms or additional binary variables without changing the DTG core.  

---

### End of formulation  

The MILP above provides a **linear, solvable** representation of conflict detection and resolution under ETCS Level‑2 DTG signalling, explicitly accounting for **speed‑dependent braking distances** and **train‑specific brake‑indication points**, while still allowing **re‑ordering** and **rerouting** decisions to minimise overall delay.

Based on your input, generate a complete, linear model with variables, objective function and constraints.

Conflict detection and resolution models typically consider train separation distances based on a number of blocks corresponding to conventional fixed-block signalling systems. However, modern distance-to-go railway signalling systems, such as the European Train Control System (ETCS), use braking curve supervision, resulting in train- and speed-dependent train separation distances. This paper proposes a modelling approach that incorporates train- and speed-dependent brake indication points and the resulting blocking times, enhancing conflict detection and resolution models for distance-to-go signalling. By integrating these enhancements into the state-of-the-art RECIFE-MILP model, a mixed integer linear programming formulation explicitly representing fixed-block distance-to-go signalling is obtained. The enhanced model is evaluated considering the state-of-practice fixed-block distance-to-go signalling system ETCS Level 2, and is compared with the original model for conventional fixed-block signalling in two real-world case studies. Results show that the shorter train separation under distance-to-go signalling leads to different rescheduling decisions, including a significant number of reroutings and some reorderings. With that, reductions in total train delay are achieved for 98% and 55% of the respective case study instances. While the mean reductions are below 1%, reductions of up to 7% are observed. These findings illustrate the operational relevance of incorporating distance-to-go principles into conflict detection and resolution modelling.

Introduction

Worldwide, railways are experiencing a continuously increasing travel demand. The existing railway networks have limited capacity and fewer and fewer extension possibilities due to the costly and land-consuming infrastructure. Especially at capacity bottlenecks such as in and around stations, extensions are often not available. To fulfil future railway demand in a different way, advanced signalling systems such as distance-to-go (DTG) systems are developed as capacityincreasing alternatives to conventional fixed-block multi-aspect signalling with automatic train protection systems.

In conventional fixed-block systems, the track is partitioned into blocks of fixed lengths which can be occupied by at most one train at a time.

The block entries are protected by trackside multi-aspect signals which indicate whether an approaching train can proceed, needs to start braking or is required to stop. The automatic train protection system supervises that the trains follow the signal aspects and intervenes when a train does not start braking after a brake indication. Hence, train separation distances are determined based on a number of blocks of fixed length.

Fixed-block DTG systems feature radio-based cab signalling and continuous braking curve supervision from the train front position to the block (or section) entry corresponding to the train’s end of movement authority (MA), i.e., the permission to move to a specific location under supervision. With this, brake indications no longer need to be provided at the entry of a block. Moreover, train separation distances become speed-dependent due to the approach distance to the first occupied block being based on the train’s absolute braking distance.

For effective railway operations, real-time traffic management is crucial. In case of small delays originating from variations in rolling stock, dwell times and driver behaviour, traffic management can apply rescheduling measures such as retiming, reordering and local rerouting to resolve track conflicts while minimising the delay propagation in the network. To support human dispatchers in taking mathematically optimised rescheduling decisions, conflict detection and resolution (CDR) models describing variants of the real-time railway traffic management or rescheduling problem are developed (Cacchiani et al., 2014; Pellegrini et al., 2014). In short, the problem can be formally described as follows: given a railway network and timetable together with delayed events, find a new timetable by rescheduling trains such that all track conflicts are resolved and total delay (or other relevant objective) is minimised.

The existing CDR models mostly refer to conventional fixed-block signalling systems. As a result, they are typically microscopic models that inherently rely on the discretisation of the track into fixed blocks. Moreover, they generally neglect changes in the speed profile to fit the adjusted timetable (Reynolds et al., 2022). Hence, these models cannot accurately capture the speed-dependent separation distances typical for DTG signalling due to the implementation of braking curve supervision (Versluis et al., 2024).

In this paper, we address the research gap regarding CDR for DTG signalling by developing a CDR model for DTG and applying it to assess the operational relevance of modelling CDR for DTG. To obtain a model that represents and identifies optimised rescheduling decisions for DTG railway operations, we propose enhancements for existing CDR models. The enhancements include the introduction of speed profile options and train blocking times considering train- and speed-dependent braking distances. These two enhancements are significant as they are crucial in enabling the modelling of train- and speed-dependent brake indication points in CDR models. As a proof of concept, we incorporate the enhancements into the state-of-the-art CDR model of RECIFE-MILP (Pellegrini et al., 2015), together with a distinction between switches and the rest of the track. The resulting model is assessed through a comparative analysis with the original one for conventional fixed-block signalling in two case studies, specifically in terms of total train delay and rescheduling decisions.

With this, the main contributions of the paper are:

• A modelling approach for enhancing conflict detection and resolution models to apply to distance-to-go signalling, introducing train- and speed-dependent train separation and brake indication points.

• A mixed-integer linear programming model for conflict detection and resolution under distance-to-go signalling, obtained by integrating distance-to-go principles into the state-of-the-art RECIFE-MILP model.

• A comparative analysis illustrating the operational relevance of incorporating distance-to-go principles into conflict detection and resolution modelling, as different rescheduling decisions achieving reductions in total train delay are proposed.

The paper is organised as follows. In Section 2, the state-of-the-art related to the modelling of CDR for DTG signalling is provided.

Section 3 describes the enhancement approach for CDR models to describe DTG signalling.

The mathematical formulation of the fixed-block CDR model RECIFE-MILP enhanced for DTG signalling is presented in Section 4. Section 5 presents the results of the comparative analysis. Finally, Section 6 concludes the paper. State-of-the-art in conflict detection and resolution for distance-to-go signalling In this section, we provide an overview of the state-of-the-art relevant for the topic of modelling CDR under DTG signalling. Section 2.1 focuses on DTG signalling as the de-facto standard in the development of next-generation signalling systems. Section 2.2 provides an overview on modelling approaches for CDR existing in the literature.

2.1 Distance-to-go signalling systems In the development of next-generation signalling systems, DTG is the de-facto standard. For the mainline railways, DTG signalling is included within the European Train Control System (ETCS) and the Chinese Train Control System (CTCS). For metro lines, Communication-Based Train Control (CBTC) applies DTG signalling principles. Examples of deployed DTG systems are the fixed-block ETCS Level 2 with Trackside Train Detection (TTD) and the similar CTCS Level 3. The latter is designed for the Chinese high-speed (up to 300 km/h) railway lines (Xu et al., 2017). In this paper, we focus on ETCS Level 2 with TTD, hereafter referred to as ETCS L2, which is implemented on freight and passenger railways throughout the world (European Rail Supply Industry Association, 2022).

To enable cab signalling, ETCS L2 features radio communication between a radio block centre on the trackside and the trains as follows. The radio block centre receives train position information from a train. This information supports the request for a route extension to the interlocking system. Based on safety logic and input from TTD, the interlocking system sets and locks a new route for the train. As a next step, the radio block centre updates the MA before sending it to the train. With the received MA, the train recomputes and supervises a dynamic speed profile including continuous braking curves.

Corresponding to the braking curves, the brake indication point for a train can lie anywhere along the track. The end of authority, however, is consistently set at the end of a block or TTD section (TDS). The TDSs correspond to the parts of the track in which the presence of a train is automatically detected. Whether the end of authority corresponds to a block or TDS depends on the implemented ETCS L2 variant. It can also depend on whether it is on the open line, in a station or around switches. A schematic representation of the ETCS L2 system is provided in Figure 1. In the figure, two trains at the speed-dependent minimum separation distance are included.

Figure 1: Schematic layout of the minimum separation between two trains in a speed-distance diagram under ETCS L2 with (block) section boundaries, radio block centre (RBC) and radio communication (GSM-R). The separation is related to the brake indication point (IP) and the end of authority (EoA) depending on the braking curve.

Within ETCS and CTCS, more advanced application levels are being developed, but not yet deployed.

In particular, ETCS Level 2 with onboard train integrity monitoring (TIM), previously known as ETCS Level 3. This allows the end of authority to be located at the end of the last free virtual (non-physical) block, e.g., in ETCS Level 2 Virtual Block, or even at a safety margin behind the rear position of a moving train, e.g., in ETCS Level 2 Moving Block (European Railway Agency, 2016).

The model must move beyond conventional fixed-block constraints by incorporating speed-dependent braking distances and train-specific brake indication points.

### Problem Context & Assumptions:
1. **Network Structure**: The network consists of a set of tracks (sections/blocks) and switches.
2. **Trains**: A set of trains $i \in \mathcal{I}$ with scheduled arrival/departure times and specific speed profiles.
3. **DTG Signalling**: Unlike fixed blocks where separation is a constant number of blocks, here the separation depends on the braking distance $d_{i,v}$ of train $i$ at speed $v$.
4. **Brake Indication Point (BIP)**: For a train $i$ following train $j$, the safety constraint is that train $i$ must not enter the braking zone of train $j$ until train $j$ has cleared a certain distance, or more accurately, the braking curve of train $i$ must be supervised such that it can stop before the end of authority (EoA) of the preceding train.
5. **Decision Variables**: 
   - $t_{i,s}$: Arrival/Departure time of train $i$ at section $s$.
   - $x_{i,j,s}$: Binary variable for reordering (1 if train $i$ precedes train $j$ on section $s$).
   - $y_{i,r}$: Binary variable for rerouting (1 if train $i$ uses route $r$).
6. **Objective**: Minimize total delay (sum of actual arrival times minus scheduled arrival times).

### Mathematical Formulation Requirements:

**Sets and Indices:**
- $\mathcal{I}$: Set of trains.
- $\mathcal{S}$: Set of track sections/blocks.
- $\mathcal{R}$: Set of available routes for each train.
- $\mathcal{P}_{i}$: Ordered sequence of sections for train $i$ in its chosen route.

**Parameters:**
- $T^{sch}_{i,s}$: Scheduled time for train $i$ at section $s$.
- $D_{i,s}$: Distance of section $s$ for train $i$.
- $V_{i,s}$: Speed of train $i$ in section $s$ (can be a set of discrete speed options to allow for speed profile optimization).
- $B_{i}(v)$: Braking distance required for train $i$ at speed $v$.
- $M$: A large positive constant (Big-M).

**Decision Variables:**
- $a_{i,s} \ge 0$: Actual arrival time of train $i$ at the end of section $s$.
- $d_{i,s} \ge 0$: Actual departure time of train $i$ from section $s$.
- $z_{i,j,s} \in \{0, 1\}$: 1 if train $i$ precedes train $j$ on section $s$, 0 otherwise.
- $r_{i,k} \in \{0, 1\}$: 1 if train $i$ chooses route $k$.

**Objective Function:**
$$\min \sum_{i \in \mathcal{I}} (a_{i, \text{destination}} - T^{sch}_{i, \text{destination}})$$

**Constraints:**
1. **Route Selection**: Each train must follow exactly one route.
   $$\sum_{k \in \mathcal{R}_i} r_{i,k} = 1 \quad \forall i \in \mathcal{I}$$

2. **Time-Distance Consistency (Speed Profiles)**:
   The travel time in a section must account for the chosen speed $v$.
   $$a_{i,s} \ge d_{i,s-1} + \frac{D_{i,s}}{V_{i,s}} \quad (\text{Simplified linear version})$$

3. **DTG Safety Separation (The Core Enhancement)**:
   For two trains $i$ and $j$ on the same section $s$, if $i$ follows $j$ ($z_{j,i,s}=1$), the arrival of $i$ at the section must be such that its braking curve is respected.
   The distance-to-go principle implies that the separation is not just "one block" but depends on the braking distance $B_i(v)$.
   $$a_{i,s} \ge a_{j,s} + \text{SafetyMargin}(B_i(v), \text{speed}) - M(1 - z_{j,i,s})$$
   *Note: In a linear model, the braking distance $B_i(v)$ should be treated as a parameter based on the selected speed profile option.*

4. **Conflict Resolution (Reordering/Rerouting)**:
   Standard MILP constraints for $z_{i,j,s}$ to ensure no two trains occupy the same space-time block simultaneously, adjusted for the DTG braking distance.

Please provide the full MILP with clear definitions of all variables, the objective, and the constraints."}

messages.content:
Below is a **complete, linear mixed‑integer programming (MILP) formulation** for Conflict‑Detection‑and‑Resolution (CDR) in a railway network that uses **Distance‑to‑Go (DTG) signalling (ETCS Level 2)**.  
The model extends the usual fixed‑block formulation by (i) using **speed‑dependent braking distances** and (ii) introducing **train‑specific Brake‑Indication‑Points (BIP)** that must be respected when a train follows another one.

---

## 1.  Sets and Indices  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| $\mathcal I$ | Set of trains, indexed by $i$ |
| $\mathcal S$ | Set of track sections (blocks), indexed by $s$ |
| $\mathcal R_i$ | Set of admissible routes for train $i$, indexed by $k$ |
| $\mathcal P_{i,k}\subseteq\mathcal S$ | Ordered list of sections that compose route $k$ for train $i$ |
| $\mathcal V_{i,s}$ | Discrete speed options that train $i$ may use in section $s$, indexed by $v$ |
| $\mathcal J_i$ | Set of trains that can ever share a section with train $i$ (i.e. $j\in\mathcal J_i$ if $\exists s$ with $s\in\mathcal P_{i,k}$ and $s\in\mathcal P_{j,\ell}$ for some $k,\ell$) |

---

## 2.  Parameters  

| Symbol | Meaning | Typical unit |
|--------|---------|--------------|
| $T^{\text{sch}}_{i,s}$ | Scheduled time at the **end** of section $s$ for train $i$ | s |
| $D_{i,s}$ | Physical length of section $s$ (for train $i$) | m |
| $L_{i,s}$ | Length of the **Brake‑Indication‑Point** (BIP) of train $i$ measured from the downstream end of section $s$ (the distance that must be cleared before the following train can enter) | m |
| $B_i(v)$ | Braking distance of train $i$ when travelling at speed $v$ (parameter, pre‑computed from the train’s braking curve) | m |
| $V_{i,s}^{v}$ | Speed value (in m/s) of option $v\in\mathcal V_{i,s}$ | m/s |
| $M$ | Large positive constant (big‑M) – must dominate any feasible time difference (e.g. $M=10^5$ s) |
| $\Delta^{\text{min}}$ | Minimum admissible headway (e.g. signalling reaction time) | s |
| $c_{i}$ | Penalty weight for train $i$’s delay (usually $c_i=1$) | – |

---

## 3.  Decision Variables  

| Symbol | Type | Meaning |
|--------|------|---------|
| $a_{i,s}\ge 0$ | Continuous | **Actual arrival time** of train $i$ at the **down‑stream end** of section $s$ |
| $d_{i,s}\ge 0$ | Continuous | **Actual departure time** of train $i$ from the **up‑stream end** of section $s$ (i.e. the time it clears the section) |
| $v_{i,s}^{v}\in\{0,1\}$ | Binary | 1 if train $i$ uses speed option $v$ in section $s$, 0 otherwise (only one speed per section) |
| $r_{i,k}\in\{0,1\}$ | Binary | 1 if train $i$ follows route $k\in\mathcal R_i$, 0 otherwise |
| $z_{i,j,s}\in\{0,1\}$ | Binary | 1 if **train $i$ precedes train $j$** on section $s$ (i.e. $i$ is ahead of $j$), 0 otherwise |
| $u_{i,j,s}\in\{0,1\}$ | Binary | 1 if **both** trains $i$ and $j$ occupy section $s$ (used to activate the separation constraint only when they share the section) |

---

## 4.  Objective  

Minimise total (weighted) delay at the final destination of every train  

\[
\boxed{
\min \; \sum_{i\in\mathcal I} c_i\Bigl(a_{i,s_i^{\text{dest}}}-T^{\text{sch}}_{i,s_i^{\text{dest}}}\Bigr)
}
\]

where $s_i^{\text{dest}}$ is the last section of the route actually selected for train $i$ (the destination section).

---

## 5.  Model Constraints  

### 5.1  Route‑selection  

\[
\sum_{k\in\mathcal R_i} r_{i,k}=1 \qquad\forall i\in\mathcal I \tag{R1}
\]

### 5.2  Section‑membership linking  

A train can only have timing variables on sections that belong to the chosen route.

\[
a_{i,s}\le M\Bigl(\sum_{k\in\mathcal R_i} r_{i,k}\,\mathbf 1_{s\in\mathcal P_{i,k}}\Bigr) \qquad\forall i,s \tag{R2}
\]
\[
d_{i,s}\le M\Bigl(\sum_{k\in\mathcal R_i} r_{i,k}\,\mathbf 1_{s\in\mathcal P_{i,k}}\Bigr) \qquad\forall i,s \tag{R3}
\]

(If $s$ does **not** belong to the selected route, the RHS becomes 0 and the variables are forced to 0.)

### 5.3  Exactly one speed option per traversed section  

\[
\sum_{v\in\mathcal V_{i,s}} v_{i,s}^{v}= \sum_{k\in\mathcal R_i} r_{i,k}\,\mathbf 1_{s\in\mathcal P_{i,k}} \qquad\forall i,s \tag{S1}
\]

Thus a speed is chosen **iff** the section is travelled.

### 5.4  Time‑distance consistency (travel time)  

For each train and each traversed section $s$ (with predecessor section $p(s)$ in the chosen route)

\[
a_{i,s}\;\ge\; d_{i,p(s)}\;+\;\sum_{v\in\mathcal V_{i,s}} \frac{D_{i,s}}{V_{i,s}^{v}}\,v_{i,s}^{v} \qquad\forall i,\;s\in\mathcal P_{i,k},\;k\in\mathcal R_i \tag{T1}
\]

If a section is the first one of a route, $d_{i,p(s)}$ is replaced by the train’s scheduled departure from its origin (or a given release time).

### 5.5  Minimum dwell / clearance inside a section  

A train must stay in a section at least long enough to travel it at the chosen speed, plus a small signalling reaction time $\Delta^{\text{min}}$:

\[
d_{i,s}\;\ge\; a_{i,s}\;+\;\Delta^{\text{min}} \qquad\forall i,s \tag{T2}
\]

### 5.6  Co‑existence indicator  

\[
u_{i,j,s}\;\ge\; z_{i,j,s} \qquad\forall i<j,\;s\in\mathcal S \tag{U1}
\]
\[
u_{i,j,s}\;\ge\; z_{j,i,s} \qquad\forall i<j,\;s\in\mathcal S \tag{U2}
\]
\[
u_{i,j,s}\;\le\; z_{i,j,s}+z_{j,i,s} \qquad\forall i<j,\;s\in\mathcal S \tag{U3}
\]

Thus $u_{i,j,s}=1$ exactly when the two trains use the same section (the ordering variables become relevant only then).

### 5.7  Ordering (precedence) on a shared section  

For every unordered pair of trains that may share a section:

\[
z_{i,j,s}+z_{j,i,s}=u_{i,j,s}\qquad\forall i<j,\;s\in\mathcal S \tag{O1}
\]

If the section is not shared ($u_{i,j,s}=0$) both ordering binaries are forced to 0.

### 5.8  **DTG safety separation – core enhancement**  

When train $i$ follows train $j$ on section $s$ ($z_{j,i,s}=1$) the **arrival** of $i$ must be delayed enough so that, even if $i$ brakes at the speed it will use in $s$, it can stop **before** the **Brake‑Indication‑Point** of $j$ (i.e. before $j$’s *end‑of‑authority*).  
The required time head‑way is the **braking time** needed to cover the distance $B_i(V_{i,s})+L_{j,s}$, where $L_{j,s}$ is the BIP length of the leading train.

Because $B_i(v)$ and $L_{j,s}$ are parameters, the head‑way can be expressed linearly as a *time* using the speed actually chosen by train $i$:

\[
\underbrace{\frac{B_i\!\bigl(V_{i,s}^{v}\bigr)+L_{j,s}}{V_{i,s}^{v}}}_{\displaystyle \text{Braking\;time for option }v}
\;\;=\;\; \tau_{i,s}^{v}\quad\forall v\in\mathcal V_{i,s}
\]

(Pre‑compute $\tau_{i,s}^{v}$ for every train, section and speed option.)

The DTG separation constraint becomes

\[
a_{i,s}\;\ge\; a_{j,s}\;+\;\sum_{v\in\mathcal V_{i,s}}\tau_{i,s}^{v}\,v_{i,s}^{v}
\;-\;M\bigl(1-z_{j,i,s}\bigr) \qquad\forall i\neq j,\;s\in\mathcal S \tag{D1}
\]

Explanation:

* If $z_{j,i,s}=1$ (i follows $j$) the big‑M term disappears and the inequality enforces the required braking‑time head‑way.  
* If $z_{j,i,s}=0$ the RHS is reduced by $M$, making the constraint non‑binding.

A symmetric version for the opposite order is automatically covered by the pair of constraints generated for the ordered pair $(i,j)$ and $(j,i)$.

### 5.9  No‑overlap in the same physical space (optional tighter bound)  

Because the DTG rule already guarantees that the following train can stop before the BIP of the leading train, an additional “one‑train‑per‑section” constraint is not strictly needed.  
If the practitioner still wants an explicit occupancy limit (e.g. to model signalling system capacity), the classic big‑M formulation can be added:

\[
d_{i,s}\;\le\; a_{j,s}\;-\;\Delta^{\text{min}} \;+\;M\bigl(1-z_{i,j,s}\bigr) \qquad\forall i\neq j,\;s\in\mathcal S \tag{O2}
\]

Together with (O1) this forces the two trains to be temporally separated by at least $\Delta^{\text{min}}$ when they are ordered.

### 5.10  Destination‑time definition (for the objective)  

Let $s_i^{\text{dest}}$ be the last section of the selected route of train $i$:

\[
s_i^{\text{dest}} = \sum_{k\in\mathcal R_i} k_{\text{last}}\,r_{i,k} \qquad\forall i\in\mathcal I
\]

where $k_{\text{last}}$ is the index of the last section in route $k$.  
Then the objective uses $a_{i,s_i^{\text{dest}}}$ as defined above.

---

## 6.  Summary of the Linear MILP  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;&\sum_{i\in\mathcal I} c_i\bigl(a_{i,s_i^{\text{dest}}}-T^{\text{sch}}_{i,s_i^{\text{dest}}}\bigr)\\[4pt]
\text{s.t. } &\text{(R1)–(R3)} &&\text{route selection and section activation}\\
&\text{(S1)} &&\text{exactly one speed per traversed section}\\
&\text{(T1)} &&\text{travel‑time consistency}\\
&\text{(T2)} &&\text{minimum dwell / clearance}\\
&\text{(U1)–(U3), (O1)} &&\text{co‑existence and ordering binaries}\\
&\text{(D1)} &&\text{DTG safety separation (core enhancement)}\\
&\text{(O2)} &&\text{optional explicit occupancy limit}\\
& a_{i,s},d_{i,s}\ge 0,\; v_{i,s}^{v},r_{i,k},z_{i,j,s},u_{i,j,s}\in\{0,1\}.
\end{aligned}
\]

All constraints are **linear**; the only non‑linear looking elements are the products $ \tau_{i,s}^{v}\,v_{i,s}^{v}$, but $v_{i,s}^{v}$ is binary, so the product is linear (a weighted sum of constants). The big‑M terms keep the model mixed‑integer.

---

## 7.  How the Model Captures the DTG Features  

| Feature | How it appears in the formulation |
|--------|-----------------------------------|
| **Speed‑dependent braking distance** | Parameter $B_i(v)$ (or pre‑computed $\tau_{i,s}^{v}$) is used inside constraint (D1). The head‑way depends on the *actual* speed chosen for the following train. |
| **Brake‑Indication‑Point (BIP)** | Parameter $L_{j,s}$ (distance from the downstream end of section $s$ that the leading train must clear) is added to the braking distance of the following train, again inside (D1). |
| **Dynamic separation (DTG)** | Instead of a fixed block count, (D1) enforces a **time head‑way** equal to the time needed for the following train to brake over $B_i(v)+L_{j,s}$, i.e. a true distance‑to‑go safety margin. |
| **Re‑ordering** | Binary $z_{i,j,s}$ decides which train is ahead on a shared section. The model can flip the order (by changing $z$) to resolve conflicts. |
| **Rerouting** | Binary $r_{i,k}$ chooses a route; the set of sections that become active for a train is linked to $r_{i,k}$ (constraints R2‑R3). |
| **Delay minimisation** | Objective penalises the difference between the actual arrival at the destination and the scheduled arrival, encouraging the solver to keep trains as close as possible to the timetable while respecting DTG safety. |

---

## 8.  Practical Modelling Tips  

1. **Big‑M sizing** – Choose $M$ just large enough to dominate the longest possible schedule deviation (e.g. $M = 10^4$ s). Too large values harm numerical stability.  
2. **Pre‑computation of $\tau$** – For every train $i$, section $s$, and speed option $v$, compute  
   \[
   \tau_{i,s}^{v}= \frac{B_i(V_{i,s}^{v})+L_{\text{max}}}{V_{i,s}^{v}}
   \]  
   where $L_{\text{max}}$ is the longest BIP among all trains that may be ahead on $s$. This keeps the model linear.  
3. **Sparse pair set** – In realistic networks only a tiny fraction of train pairs ever share a section; generate $\mathcal J_i$ accordingly to keep the number of $z$ and $u$ variables manageable.  
4. **Route‑specific BIPs** – If a BIP length depends on the route (e.g. different switch geometry), store $L_{j,s,k}$ and use the selected route binary $r_{j,k}$ to pick the correct value inside (D1).  
5. **Extensions** – The model can be enriched with (i) energy‑optimal speed selection, (ii) platform dwell‑time windows, (iii) passenger‑connection penalties – all by adding linear terms or additional binary variables without changing the DTG core.  

---

### End of formulation  

The MILP above provides a **linear, solvable** representation of conflict detection and resolution under ETCS Level‑2 DTG signalling, explicitly accounting for **speed‑dependent braking distances** and **train‑specific brake‑indication points**, while still allowing **re‑ordering** and **rerouting** decisions to minimise overall delay.

response.content:
The provided model is a complete, linear mixed-integer programming (MILP) formulation designed for Conflict Detection and Resolution (CDR) in railway networks utilizing **Distance-to-Go (DTG)** signalling (such as ETCS Level 2). 

Unlike conventional models that rely on fixed block counts, this model incorporates **speed-dependent braking distances** and **Brake-Indication-Points (BIP)** to enable more efficient rescheduling decisions, such as rerouting and reordering, which are critical for maximizing capacity in modern signalling environments.

---

## 1. Sets and Indices
*   $\mathcal{I}$: Set of trains, indexed by $i$.
*   $\mathcal{S}$: Set of track sections (blocks), indexed by $s$.
*   $\mathcal{R}_i$: Set of available routes for train $i$, indexed by $k$.
*   $\mathcal{P}_{i,k} \subseteq \mathcal{S}$: The ordered sequence of sections constituting route $k$ for train $i$.
*   $\mathcal{V}_{i,s}$: Set of discrete speed profile options for train $i$ in section $s$, indexed by $v$.
*   $\mathcal{J}_i$: Set of trains $j$ that may share a section with train $i$.

## 2. Parameters
*   $T^{\text{sch}}_{i,s}$: Scheduled arrival time of train $i$ at the end of section $s$.
*   $D_{i,s}$: Physical length of section $s$ for train $i$.
*   $L_{j,s}$: Distance from the end of section $s$ to the Brake-Indication-Point (BIP) of train $j$.
*   $B_i(v)$: Braking distance required for train $i$ at speed $v$.
*   $V_{i,s}^{v}$: Velocity value associated with speed option $v$ for train $i$ in section $s$.
*   $\tau_{i,s}^{v}$: Pre-computed time headway required for train $i$ at speed $v$ in section $s$ to safely respect the braking curve: $\tau_{i,s}^{v} = \frac{B_i(v) + L_{j,s}}{V_{i,s}^{v}}$.
*   $M$: A sufficiently large constant (Big-M) for logical constraints.
*   $c_i$: Weighting factor for the delay of train $i$.

## 3. Decision Variables
*   $a_{i,s} \ge 0$: Actual arrival time of train $i$ at the downstream end of section $s$.
*   $d_{i,s} \ge 0$: Actual departure time of train $i$ from the upstream end of section $s$.
*   $r_{i,k} \in \{0, 1\}$: 1 if train $i$ selects route $k$; 0 otherwise.
*   $v_{i,s}^{v} \in \{0, 1\}$: 1 if train $i$ uses speed option $v$ in section $s$; 0 otherwise.
*   $z_{i,j,s} \in \{0, 1\}$: 1 if train $i$ precedes train $j$ on section $s$; 0 otherwise.
*   $u_{i,j,s} \in \{0, 1\}$: 1 if both trains $i$ and $j$ occupy section $s$.

## 4. Objective Function
Minimize the total weighted delay of all trains at their respective destinations:
$$\min \sum_{i \in \mathcal{I}} c_i \left( a_{i, \text{dest}(i)} - T^{\text{sch}}_{i, \text{dest}(i)} \right)$$

## 5. Constraints

### 5.1 Route and Speed Selection
Each train must select exactly one route, and if a route is selected, exactly one speed must be chosen for every section in that route:
$$\sum_{k \in \mathcal{R}_i} r_{i,k} = 1 \quad \forall i \in \mathcal{I} \tag{1}$$
$$\sum_{v \in \mathcal{V}_{i,s}} v_{i,s}^{v} = \sum_{k \in \mathcal{R}_i} r_{i,k} \cdot \mathbb{1}(s \in \mathcal{P}_{i,k}) \quad \forall i \in \mathcal{I}, s \in \mathcal{S} \tag{2}$$

### 5.2 Time-Distance Consistency
The arrival time at the end of a section must account for the travel time at the chosen speed and the departure from the previous section:
$$a_{i,s} \ge d_{i, \text{prev}(s)} + \sum_{v \in \mathcal{V}_{i,s}} \left( \frac{D_{i,s}}{V_{i,s}^{v}} \right) v_{i,s}^{v} \quad \forall i \in \mathcal{I}, s \in \mathcal{P}_{i,k} \tag{3}$$
*(Note: The term $\frac{D_{i,s}}{V_{i,s}^{v}}$ is a constant parameter for each $v$, maintaining linearity.)*

### 5.3 DTG Safety Separation (Core Enhancement)
If train $i$ follows train $j$ on section $s$ ($z_{j,i,s}=1$), the arrival of train $i$ must be separated by the time required to cover the speed-dependent braking distance and the leading train's BIP:
$$a_{i,s} \ge a_{j,s} + \sum_{v \in \mathcal{V}_{i,s}} \tau_{i,s}^{v} \cdot v_{i,s}^{v} - M(1 - z_{j,i,s}) \quad \forall i, j \in \mathcal{I}, s \in \mathcal{S} \tag{4}$$

### 5.4 Conflict Resolution (Reordering and Rerouting)
To allow reordering, the model uses binary precedence variables. For any two trains $i$ and $j$ that could share a section $s$:
$$z_{i,j,s} + z_{j,i,s} \ge u_{i,j,s} \quad \forall i, j \in \mathcal{I}, s \in \mathcal{S} \tag{5}$$
Where $u_{i,j,s}$ is 1 if both trains are assigned to section $s$ via their chosen routes:
$$u_{i,j,s} \le \sum_{k \in \mathcal{R}_i} r_{i,k} \cdot \mathbb{1}(s \in \mathcal{P}_{i,k}) \quad \text{and} \quad u_{i,j,s} \le \sum_{\ell \in \mathcal{R}_j} r_{j,\ell} \cdot \mathbb{1}(s \in \mathcal{P}_{j,\ell}) \tag{6}$$

### 5.5 Logical Constraints
Ensure timing variables are only active for sections on the selected route:
$$a_{i,s} \le M \sum_{k \in \mathcal{R}_i} r_{i,k} \cdot \mathbb{1}(s \in \mathcal{P}_{i,k}) \quad \forall i \in \mathcal{I}, s \in \mathcal{S} \tag{7}$$
$$d_{i,s} \le M \sum_{k \in \mathcal{R}_i} r_{i,k} \cdot \mathbb{1}(s \in \mathcal{P}_{i,k}) \quad \forall i \in \mathcal{I}, s \in \mathcal{S} \tag{8}$$

---

## 6. Assumptions
1.  **Discrete Speed Profiles**: Speed is modeled as a set of discrete constant-speed options per section to maintain linearity.
2.  **Pre-computed Braking**: The braking distance $B_i(v)$ is assumed to be a known function of the train's characteristics and the chosen speed.
3.  **Fixed Infrastructure**: The track layout and the existence of specific routes are predefined.
4.  **Linearity**: The product of a binary variable ($v_{i,s}^{v}$) and a constant ($\tau_{i,s}^{v}$) is used to represent the speed-dependent component, ensuring the model remains a MILP.

*   $\mathcal{R}_i$: Set of available routes for train $i$, indexed by $k$.
*   $\mathcal{P}_{i,k} \subseteq \mathcal{S}$: The ordered sequence of sections constituting route $k$ for train $i$.
*   $\mathcal{V}_{i,s}$: Set of discrete speed profile options for train $i$ in section $s$, indexed by $v$.
*   $\mathcal{J}_i$: Set of trains $j$ that may share a section with train $i$.

## 2. Parameters
*   $T^{\text{sch}}_{i,s}$: Scheduled arrival time of train $i$ at the end of section $s$.
*   $D_{i,s}$: Physical length of section $s$ for train $i$.
*   $L_{j,s}$: Distance from the end of section $s$ to the Brake-Indication-Point (BIP) of train $j$.
*   $B_i(v)$: Braking distance required for train $i$ at speed $v$.
*   $V_{i,s}^{v}$: Velocity value associated with speed option $v$ for train $i$ in section $s$.
*   $\tau_{i,s}^{v}$: Pre-computed time headway required for train $i$ at speed $v$ in section $s$ to safely respect the braking curve: $\tau_{i,s}^{v} = \frac{B_i(v) + L_{j,s}}{V_{i,s}^{v}}$.
*   $M$: A sufficiently large constant (Big-M) for logical constraints.
*   $c_i$: Weighting factor for the delay of train $i$.

## 3. Decision Variables
*   $a_{i,s} \ge 0$: Actual arrival time of train $i$ at the downstream end of section $s$.
*   $d_{i,s} \ge 0$: Actual departure time of train $i$ from the upstream end of section $s$.
*   $r_{i,k} \in \{0, 1\}$: 1 if train $i$ selects route $k$; 0 otherwise.
*   $v_{i,s}^{v} \in \{0, 1\}$: 1 if train $i$ uses speed option $v$ in section $s$; 0 otherwise.
*   $z_{i,j,s} \in \{0, 1\}$: 1 if train $i$ precedes train $j$ on section $s$; 0 otherwise.
*   $u_{i,j,s} \in \{0, 1\}$: 1 if both trains $i$ and $j$ occupy section $s$.

## 4. Objective Function
Minimize the total weighted delay of all trains at their respective destinations:
$$\min \sum_{i \in \mathcal{I}} c_i \left( a_{i, \text{dest}(i)} - T^{\text{sch}}_{i, \text{dest}(i)} \right)$$

## 5. Constraints

### 5.1 Route and Speed Selection
Each train must select exactly one route, and if a route is selected, exactly one speed must be chosen for every section in that route:
$$\sum_{k \in \mathcal{R}_i} r_{i,k} = 1 \quad \forall i \in \mathcal{I} \tag{1}$$
$$\sum_{v \in \mathcal{V}_{i,s}} v_{i,s}^{v} = \sum_{k \in \mathcal{R}_i} r_{i,k} \cdot \mathbb{1}(s \in \mathcal{P}_{i,k}) \quad \forall i \in \mathcal{I}, s \in \mathcal{S} \tag{2}$$

### 5.2 Time-Distance Consistency
The arrival time at the end of a section must account for the travel time at the chosen speed and the departure from the previous section:
$$a_{i,s} \ge d_{i, \text{prev}(s)} + \sum_{v \in \mathcal{V}_{i,s}} \left( \frac{D_{i,s}}{V_{i,s}^{v}} \right) v_{i,s}^{v} \quad \forall i \in \mathcal{I}, s \in \mathcal{P}_{i,k} \tag{3}$$
*(Note: The term $\frac{D_{i,s}}{V_{i,s}^{v}}$ is a constant parameter for each $v$, maintaining linearity.)*

### 5.3 DTG Safety Separation (Core Enhancement)
If train $i$ follows train $j$ on section $s$ ($z_{j,i,s}=1$), the arrival of train $i$ must be separated by the time required to cover the speed-dependent braking distance and the leading train's BIP:
$$a_{i,s} \ge a_{j,s} + \sum_{v \in \mathcal{V}_{i,s}} \tau_{i,s}^{v} \cdot v_{i,s}^{v} - M(1 - z_{j,i,s}) \quad \forall i, j \in \mathcal{I}, s \in \mathcal{S} \tag{4}$$

### 5.4 Conflict Resolution (Reordering and Rerouting)
To allow reordering, the model uses binary precedence variables. For any two trains $i$ and $j$ that could share a section $s$:
$$z_{i,j,s} + z_{j,i,s} \ge u_{i,j,s} \quad \forall i, j \in \mathcal{I}, s \in \mathcal{S} \tag{5}$$
Where $u_{i,j,s}$ is 1 if both trains are assigned to section $s$ via their chosen routes:
$$u_{i,j,s} \le \sum_{k \in \mathcal{R}_i} r_{i,k} \cdot \mathbb{1}(s \in \mathcal{P}_{i,k}) \quad \text{and} \quad u_{i,j,s} \le \sum_{\ell \in \mathcal{R}_j} r_{j,\ell} \cdot \mathbb{1}(s \in \mathcal{P}_{j,\ell}) \tag{6}$$

### 5.5 Logical Constraints
Ensure timing variables are only active for sections on the selected route:
$$a_{i,s} \le M \sum_{k \in \mathcal{R}_i} r_{i,k} \cdot \mathbb{1}(s \in \mathcal{P}_{i,k}) \quad \forall i \in \mathcal{I}, s \in \mathcal{S} \tag{7}$$
$$d_{i,s} \le M \sum_{k \in \mathcal{R}_i} r_{i,k} \cdot \mathbb{1}(s \in \mathcal{P}_{i,k}) \quad \forall i \in \mathcal{I}, s \in \mathcal{S} \tag{8}$$

---

## 6. Assumptions
1.  **Discrete Speed Profiles**: Speed is modeled as a set of discrete constant-speed options per section to maintain linearity.
2.  **Pre-computed Braking**: The braking distance $B_i(v)$ is assumed to be a known function of the train's characteristics and the chosen speed.
3.  **Fixed Infrastructure**: The track layout and the existence of specific routes are predefined.
4.  **Linearity**: The product of a binary variable ($v_{i,s}^{v}$) and a constant ($\tau_{i,s}^{v}$) is used to represent the speed-dependent component, ensuring the model remains a MILP.
